name: API 101 — quiz
abstract: Ten questions to check what you learned about application programming interfaces.
courseDescription: Notes, slides, and a quiz about application programming interfaces, the connections that let County systems share data and services.

grades.name: A
grades.message: Excellent. You can ask good questions about who owns an API and who may use it.

grades.name: B
grades.message: Strong work. Keep asking how an API is described and how users hear about changes.

grades.name: C
grades.message: A sound start. Read the explanations, then check the notes for the ones you missed.

grades.name: D
grades.message: Go back to the key terms and the do’s and don’ts in the notes, then try again.

grades.name: F
grades.message: Start with the notes. Then take the quiz again.

questions.text: What does a vendor's API let County systems do?

options.text: Skip the contract with the vendor.
Make the product free to use.
Connect to the product and share its data.
Hide the product from staff.

questions.hint: Think about connecting products you buy to your other systems.
questions.explanation: Why it matters says a vendor's API lets County systems connect to the products you buy and share their data.

questions.text: What does an API that is not written down give the people who use it?

options.text: A faster connection
A new owner
No guarantee
A public audience

questions.hint: Think about what users can count on.
questions.explanation: Problem says an API that is not written down comes with no guarantee for the people who use it.

questions.text: Which step helps other teams and vendors know how to use an API?

options.text: Keep it private and tell no one.
Let each user work it out alone.
Change it often so users stay alert.
Describe it in a shared standard such as OpenAPI.

questions.hint: Think about a shared way to write it down.
questions.explanation: Solution says to describe each API in a shared standard such as OpenAPI.

options.text: A guide that explains a whole system.
A place where a system can be reached to get a kind of data or action.
A person who owns an API.
A rule that bans public use.

questions.hint: Think of a place you can reach.
questions.explanation: Key terms defines an endpoint as one place where a system can be reached to get a certain kind of data or action.

questions.text: Which kind of API can only chosen business partners use?

options.text: A private API
An open API
A partner API
A deprecated API

questions.explanation: Key terms defines a partner API as a connection that only chosen business partners may use.

questions.text: A deprecated part of an API is one that users should plan to move away from.
questions.hint: Think about a part that is likely to change or end.
questions.explanation: Key terms defines deprecated as marked as likely to change or end, so users should plan to move away from it.

options.text: A new version every year
A named owner
A public audience
A hidden description

questions.hint: Think about who is in charge.
questions.explanation: Do’s and don’ts says to name an owner for every API.

questions.text: It is fine to change an API without telling the people who use it.
questions.hint: Think about the people who rely on it.
questions.explanation: Do’s and don’ts says to warn users before you change or retire an API.

questions.text: Which is a good question to ask about a product you want to buy?

options.text: How many colors does its screen use?
Does it have an API, and is that described in writing?
Can we skip asking about it?
Who can we keep from asking about it?

questions.hint: Think about connecting it to your other systems.
questions.explanation: Questions to ask includes asking whether a product has an API and whether it is described in writing.

questions.text: Which statement belongs on a checklist for an API?

options.text: Users are told before it changes or ends.
Only one person knows how it works.
Its owner is not yet known.
Its rules live only in staff memory.

questions.hint: Choose the statement you want to be true.
questions.explanation: Checklist includes the item “Users are told before an API changes or ends.”
